questions.stem:
Sort each funding arrangement.

What kind of funding is this?

A bank loan of USD 10,000 repaid over three years
questions.explain: Borrowed and repaid with interest: debt.

questions.stem:
What kind of funding is this?

An angel investor gives USD 25,000 for 20% of the company
questions.explain: Money for ownership: equity.

questions.stem:
What kind of funding is this?

A cultural agency awards a production grant
questions.explain: A grant does not need repaying and gives no ownership.

questions.stem:
What kind of funding is this?

A telecom company pays to have its logo on a web series
questions.explain: Sponsorship.

questions.stem:
What kind of funding is this?

A venture capital firm buys shares in a gaming start-up
questions.explain: VC is equity financing.

questions.stem:
What kind of funding is this?

A credit union overdraft to cover equipment costs
questions.explain: An overdraft is borrowed money: debt.

questions.stem:
What kind of funding is this?

500 fans pre-order a comic book on a crowdfunding site
questions.explain: Reward-based crowdfunding and pre-sales.

questions.stem:
What kind of funding is this?

A film wins prize money at a regional festival
questions.explain: Competition prize money.

questions.stem:
Identify the creator income model in each example.

A photographer earns a fee each time a magazine uses her sunset photo.
questions.explain: Paying to use content is licensing.

questions.stem: A gamer earns a commission whenever viewers buy a headset through his link.
questions.explain: Commission through a link is affiliate marketing.

questions.stem: A music producer sells packs of drum samples as downloads.
questions.explain: Downloadable items are digital products.

questions.stem: Fans pay USD 5 a month for bonus episodes.
questions.explain: Regular payment for extras is a paid membership.

questions.stem: A food vlogger is paid by a supermarket to feature its products in one video.
questions.explain: A brand paying for sponsored content is a brand partnership.

questions.stem: The Saint Lucian game studio Pitons Play has a prototype mobile game, no income yet and plans to expand across the region. The founders are willing to give up some ownership for expertise. Which source of funding is MOST suitable?
options: A five-year bank loan with fixed monthly repayments
An angel investor who provides equity funding and mentoring

questions.stem:
Classify each way of earning using the four creator income models.

A Guyanese cooking channel earns from adverts shown before its videos.
questions.explain: Ads served on content: advertising revenue.

questions.stem: A fitness creator gets a commission each time a follower uses her discount code.
questions.explain: Affiliate marketing is part of brand partnerships in the notes.

questions.stem: A photographer sells a six-week online course in mobile photography.
questions.explain: An online course sold directly to the community.

questions.stem: A cartoonist sells T-shirts printed with her characters.
questions.explain: Branded merchandise.

questions.stem: A TV station pays a filmmaker each time it airs her drone footage.
questions.explain: Licensing content.

questions.stem:
From the Funding Models exercise

Each feature below matches ONE funding method best. Choose it. Then open the full tick table, where some features match several methods and you tick every one that applies.

Must be repaid with interest regardless of success.
questions.explain: A loan is debt: you repay it with interest even if the project fails.

questions.stem: Targeted at high-growth projects; can scale fast with firm support.
questions.explain: Venture capital firms back high-growth businesses with large sums and support. Angels are individuals, usually investing less, earlier.

questions.stem: Funding in exchange for visibility; may need to fit a brand’s image.
questions.explain: Sponsors pay in cash or kind for exposure, so your content must suit their brand.

questions.stem: Self-funded; full creative freedom but the budget can be limited.
questions.explain: Bootstrapping uses your own savings or early sales: total freedom, small budget.

questions.stem: Competitive application process with proposals and reporting.
questions.explain: Grants are won through written proposals against set criteria, with reports afterwards.

questions.stem: Builds an early audience and community around your idea.
questions.explain: Only crowdfunding: backers become your first fans. Bootstrapping is self-funding, so it brings no audience.

questions.stem:
You are launching the podcast Soca Stories, interviewing veteran soca artists across the Eastern Caribbean. You need about USD 6,000 for microphones, travel and editing. Choose your funding mix.

You have no income yet and no assets. A bank offers a USD 6,000 loan at high interest, repayable from next month. A national cultural fund is accepting grant proposals for heritage projects. Which do you pursue first?
options: Take the full bank loan now.
Write a strong proposal for the cultural fund grant.

questions.stem: The fund awards USD 3,000. You have 1,500 loyal followers from your interview clips. How do you raise more?
options: Launch a crowdfunding campaign with rewards such as early episodes and signed posters.
Sell 40% of the podcast to the first investor who asks.

questions.stem: The podcast launches and grows to 10,000 monthly listeners. How do you sustain it?
options: Combine podcast ad insertion, a paid membership with bonus episodes and a brand partnership with a regional airline.
Rely entirely on one platform's payments.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem:
Judge each piece of proposal writing.

Objective: "Make a nice website for the club."
questions.explain: Not specific, measurable or time-bound.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: Objective: "By 15 March, launch a five-page website and gain 300 visitors in its first month."
questions.explain: Specific, measurable and time-bound.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: Problem statement: "We will make videos to help tourists."
questions.explain: It states the solution, not the problem.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: Evaluation: "We will measure success by comparing ticket sales before and after the campaign."
questions.explain: A clear, measurable method.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: Executive summary: three pages covering every detail.
questions.explain: An executive summary is short, often half a page.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: Why is the executive summary usually written LAST, even though it appears near the start of the proposal?
options: Because it summarises the whole proposal, which must be complete before it can be summarised accurately.
Because it is the least important section.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem:
Each sentence comes from the proposal "MoBay Safe Seas", a short-video campaign on water safety for Montego Bay's beaches. Decide which of the five groups it belongs in.

"Three drowning incidents involving visitors were reported last season, and most visitors never see the safety signs."
questions.explain: Context and the specific problem: group 02.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: "Produce six 30-second vertical videos by 15 March and reach 50,000 views by 30 April."
questions.explain: A clear, measurable objective: group 03.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: "Success will be measured by views, shares and a survey of 100 beach visitors."
questions.explain: How success will be measured is evaluation: group 04.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: "MoBay Safe Seas, prepared by Lower Six Digital Media, Hummingbird Ridge High School."
questions.explain: Project name and team: the title page, group 01.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: "Equipment hire: USD 400; captions and translation: USD 150; contingency (10%): USD 55."
questions.explain: The financial plan: group 04.

questions.topic: Writing a project proposal and budget
questions.stem: "Week 1: script and storyboard. Week 2: filming at Doctor's Cave and Cornwall Beach. Week 3: edit and caption."
questions.explain: A roadmap: the plan of action, group 03.

questions.stem:
Sort each project behaviour.

Is this typical of agile or waterfall project management?

The client sees a rough cut after two weeks and suggests changes.
questions.explain: Early, frequent feedback is agile.

questions.stem:
Is this typical of agile or waterfall project management?

Every scene is scripted and signed off before any filming begins, and the script cannot change.
questions.explain: Rigid upfront planning is waterfall.

questions.stem:
Is this typical of agile or waterfall project management?

The team works in two-week cycles.
questions.explain: Short sprints are agile.

questions.stem:
Is this typical of agile or waterfall project management?

The finished product is shown to the client only at the end.
questions.explain: Late delivery is typical of waterfall.

questions.stem:
Is this typical of agile or waterfall project management?

Spending is compared with the plan after every cycle and the budget is updated.
questions.explain: Continuous budget review is part of the agile model.

questions.stem:
Is this typical of agile or waterfall project management?

A change request late in the project is treated as a costly problem.
questions.explain: Waterfall resists late changes.

questions.stem:
Is this typical of agile or waterfall project management?

The app is released with core features first, then improved in later updates.
questions.explain: Incremental delivery is agile.

questions.stem:
You are project manager of a four-person Lower Six team making a 3-minute documentary on Anguilla's Road Salt Pond for a heritage foundation. You are using the agile model.

Planning is done and Sprint 1 begins. The camera operator wants to film every possible scene before editing anything. What do you say?
options: Let's film the opening and one interview this sprint, edit them, and show the client a rough version at the review.
Fine. We'll film everything first, then edit at the end.

questions.stem: At the Sprint 1 review, the foundation says it wants more on the pond's history, less on birds. You also find you have spent USD 60 of your USD 150 budget already. What next?
options: Ignore the feedback; we already filmed the birds.
In iteration, reorder the backlog to put history first, adjust the timeline, and update the budget to cut a non-essential drone rental.

questions.stem: In the final sprint, a team member is ill. The documentary is 90% complete and the deadline is in two days. What do you do?
options: Wait until the student returns, even if the deadline is missed.
Hold a stand-up, redistribute the remaining tasks on the Kanban board, deliver on time and report final costs.

questions.stem:
Identify which of the 4Ps each decision belongs to.

A podcast will be released on major audio platforms and the school website.
questions.explain: Where customers get it: place.

questions.stem: Premium members pay USD 3 a month.
questions.explain: What customers pay: price.

questions.stem: Each episode features a 20-minute interview and a 2-minute recipe segment.
questions.explain: What is offered: product.

questions.stem: Teaser clips will run on short-form video apps and local radio.
questions.explain: How people hear about it: promotion.

questions.stem: The game is free to download with optional in-app purchases.
questions.explain: The pricing model: price.

questions.stem: A team pitches a Caribbean history game to a panel. They present the vision, the problem, the solution, the target market, their competition and their team, then thank the panel and sit down. Which element have they MOST seriously left out?
Which statement about a sprint is CORRECT?
options: It is the final phase, when the finished project is released.
It is the phase in which the team compares the budget with actual spending for the first time.
It is a long planning period at the start of a project, before any content is made.
It is a short, time-boxed work cycle, typically one to four weeks, in which the team creates a defined piece of content.

questions.stem:
Kemar, a Lower Six student in Jamaica, is generating ideas for a short film about water conservation. Identify each technique he uses.

He writes the word "drought" and then "dust", "thirst", "desert", "silence" in a chain.
questions.explain: Each word triggers the next in a chain. That is word association.

questions.stem: He writes non-stop for five minutes about a day without water, ignoring spelling.
questions.explain: Writing continuously without stopping or editing is free writing.

questions.stem: He puts "Water" in the centre of a page with branches for home, school, farming and tourism.
questions.explain: A central idea with branches and sub-branches is a mind map.

questions.stem: His group spends ten minutes calling out ideas while one person records them all, with no criticism allowed.
questions.explain: Rapid group idea generation with judgement postponed is brainstorming.

questions.stem: He turns his favourite idea into one sentence describing the film, its audience and its mood.
questions.explain: Turning ideas into a clear, single concept statement is concept formulation.

questions.stem: The St. Kitts tour company Brimstone Trails commissioned a booking web page for cruise visitors. Which action BEST represents validation of the design?
options: The page is uploaded to the company's web server.
The team brainstorms 20 possible names for the tour packages.
Five cruise visitors are asked to book a tour on a phone prototype while the team times them and notes where they get stuck.
The designer chooses a turquoise colour scheme because it looks tropical.

questions.stem:
A design team in Barbados is reviewing its work for a new juice brand, Bajan Squeeze. Sort each design decision by the Gestalt principle it mainly uses.

Which Gestalt principle?

On the menu board, each juice name sits directly above its price, with a large gap before the next juice.
questions.explain: Closeness groups each name with its price: proximity.

questions.stem:
Which Gestalt principle?

All the "Order now" buttons on the website are the same mango-orange pill shape.
questions.explain: Shared colour and shape tell users these belong together: similarity.

questions.stem:
Which Gestalt principle?

The logo is a circle of five separate leaf shapes with gaps, yet people see a whole orange.
questions.explain: The brain completes the missing parts: closure.

questions.stem:
Which Gestalt principle?

On the flyer, the address, phone number and opening hours are grouped tightly in one corner.
questions.explain: Grouping contact details by placing them close together is proximity.

questions.stem:
Which Gestalt principle?

Every sugar-free flavour has a green label, wherever it sits on the shelf.
questions.explain: A shared colour links items that are far apart: similarity.

questions.stem:
Which Gestalt principle?

The bottle icon is drawn with a dashed outline, but it still reads as a bottle.
questions.explain: The eye fills the gaps in the outline: closure.

questions.stem:
Identify the principle at work in each example from Caribbean design work.

A logo for a turtle-protection group is a white turtle shape cut out of a solid blue circle; the white is read as the turtle.
questions.explain: The shape is formed by the relationship between object and background: figure / ground.

questions.stem: On a festival app, three event listings sit inside one shaded card labelled "Friday".
questions.explain: The shared enclosed area groups them: common region.

questions.stem: A brochure arranges photos along a curving line that follows the coastline, and the eye travels smoothly from one to the next.
questions.explain: The eye follows the smooth path: continuity.

questions.stem: A wedding invitation is perfectly mirrored left to right around a central monogram.
questions.explain: A mirrored, balanced layout is perceived as one stable unit: symmetry.

questions.stem: A designer in Nassau is making a simple A3 poster for a beach clean-up: a logo, a bold headline, one large photo and a "Sign up today" button with a QR code. Following the Z-pattern, where should the call to action go?
options: In the exact centre, on top of the photo.
Top left, before the logo, so it is seen first.
Bottom right, where the Z-pattern ends.

questions.stem: A student's poster for a Trinidad youth steel pan concert uses the same 24 pt bold type for the title, the date, the venue, the ticket price and the sponsor list. Viewers cannot tell what the poster is about. Which change BEST fixes the visual hierarchy?
options: Set the title large and bold as the primary level, the date and venue medium as secondary, and the price and sponsors small as tertiary.
Centre every line and add a decorative border.
Add more photographs so the poster looks busier and more exciting.
Make every line a different bright colour so each one stands out.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Anguilla Youth Music Fest hires your group to produce a promo campaign: one 60-second video, a set of social media graphics and a one-page website. The client wants to approve work as it goes. You have five weeks.

Which implementation model do you propose?
options: A purely cyclic model: keep redesigning everything until the client is fully happy.
A strict linear model: do everything in one sequence with no reviews until the final delivery.
A branched network for the three parts, with stepped approval checkpoints within each branch.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: At the first checkpoint, the client rejects the video storyboard: "Too much talking, not enough crowd energy." What do you do?
options: Ignore it and film the original storyboard, because the script is already written.
Loop back one step: revise the storyboard with more crowd and performance shots, then resubmit.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: In week four the website branch and the graphics branch have used different shades of orange and different fonts. How do you respond?
options: Hold a short merge meeting, agree a shared style guide (colours as hex codes, fonts, logo use) and update both branches.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Sort each project feature according to whether it belongs to a linear (waterfall) approach or an agile approach.

Linear or agile?

All requirements are fixed before any production begins.
questions.explain: Fixing everything up front is typical of the linear (waterfall) approach.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Linear or agile?

Work is delivered in two-week sprints.
questions.explain: Sprints are a core agile (scrum) practice.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Linear or agile?

The client sees the product only at final delivery.
questions.explain: In a linear model the finished product is revealed at the end.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Linear or agile?

A daily 15-minute stand-up meeting is held.
questions.explain: The daily stand-up is a scrum routine.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Linear or agile?

Priorities can change after each sprint review.
questions.explain: Adapting to feedback is the heart of agile.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Linear or agile?

A detailed schedule shows each phase in sequence from start to finish.
questions.explain: A single, sequential phase plan is characteristic of linear work.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Linear or agile?

A retrospective looks at how the team can work better next cycle.
questions.explain: Retrospectives are an agile practice for continuous improvement.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Choose the best planning artefact for each task.

Showing a client the colours, fonts and photo style for a new Bajan skincare brand.
questions.explain: Look and feel (colours, fonts, imagery) is communicated by a mood board.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: Planning the shots of a 45-second public service announcement.
questions.explain: A shot-by-shot plan over time is a storyboard.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: Planning where the menu, search bar and "Book now" button go on a tour company's app.
questions.explain: Screen layout and navigation are planned with a wireframe.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: Letting users click through a draft app to test whether booking is easy.
questions.explain: A clickable prototype lets users test the flow.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: Recording the hex codes #0B6E99 and #F4A300 for a campaign palette.
questions.explain: Colour codes belong on the mood board or in the style guide that grows from it.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
A team is designing a Barbados bus-times app. Sort each piece of work into the stage it belongs to.

Which stage?

Grey boxes and lines showing where the route map, search bar and timetable sit on the home screen.
questions.explain: Layout with placeholder shapes and no colour is a wireframe.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

A pencil sketch on paper agreeing which screens the app needs and how they link.
questions.explain: A quick sketch of structure and flow is a low-fidelity wireframe.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

A diagram mapping the content hierarchy and navigation paths, with no colours or images.
questions.explain: Information architecture is set out at the wireframe stage.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

Two full-colour versions of the home screen, one in yellow and blue and one in navy and white, for the client to choose between.
questions.explain: Static, full-colour variations for visual decisions are mock-ups.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

A static screen showing the final icons, the chosen font and real photographs of bus stops.
questions.explain: Final visual detail without interactivity is a mock-up.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

A polished set of screens handed to the developer as the visual reference for colours and spacing.
questions.explain: Mock-ups support developer handoff for the look and feel.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

Linked screens: tapping "Find my bus" opens the results and tapping a route shows its live map.
questions.explain: Clickable navigation between screens makes it a prototype.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

Five commuters try to plan a journey on a clickable version while the team notes where they hesitate.
questions.explain: Usability testing with users is done on a prototype.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
Which stage?

A clickable demonstration shown to an investor to show exactly how buying a ticket works.
questions.explain: Interactive demos for investors are prototypes.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem:
The owner of the ferry company SeaLink BVI wants an app for booking crossings between Tortola and Virgin Gorda. Nothing has been drawn yet. She must show an investor in six weeks and wants to launch in four months. You lead the design.

What do you do first?
options: Spend two weeks perfecting a full-colour mock-up of the home screen.
Ask a developer to start coding straight away to save time.
Sketch low-fidelity wireframes of the key screens and walk five commuters through the booking path.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: The wireframes are approved. Now the owner and her business partner disagree: he wants bright tropical colours; she wants a calm navy look. What next?
options: Make two mock-up variations of the home and booking screens and let them, and a few users, compare.
Leave the colours for the developer to decide while coding.

questions.topic: Methods of implementing the creative process
questions.stem: The navy design is chosen. The investor meeting is next week, and you also need to know whether tourists can book a crossing in under a minute. What do you prepare?
options: The static mock-ups only; test with real users after launch.
A clickable prototype of the booking flow (choose crossing, pick time, pay, receive ticket), tested with five tourists at the pier and then demonstrated to the investor.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Sort each design decision by the approach that BEST describes it.

Which approach does this decision mainly show?

Vendors test paper sketches of the app before any code is written.
questions.explain: Involving users early in the design is user-centred design.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Which approach does this decision mainly show?

The archive stores interviews as uncompressed WAV files so they can be remastered later.
questions.explain: Keeping high-quality masters anticipates future uses: designing for future needs.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Which approach does this decision mainly show?

A drone captures aerial footage of coastal erosion in Negril.
questions.explain: This solution is made possible by applying hardware (a drone).

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Which approach does this decision mainly show?

Button text is enlarged after older users struggle to read it.
questions.explain: Changing the design in response to users' abilities is user-centred.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Which approach does this decision mainly show?

The website is built so new languages can be added without redesigning it.
questions.explain: Planning for growth and change is designing for future needs.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Which approach does this decision mainly show?

Free open-source software is used to edit 4K footage on school laptops.
questions.explain: Choosing software creatively to make production possible is the use of hardware and software.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Which approach does this decision mainly show?

Interviewers sit with fishers on the jetty to understand how they check the weather.
questions.explain: Studying users in their context is user-centred design.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem:
Holetown Community Council asks your team to help elderly residents prepare for hurricane season. Make the best design decisions.

Where do you begin?
options: Build a hurricane app straight away; everyone has phones now.
Interview ten elderly residents and two caregivers, and observe how they currently receive news.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem: Research shows most seniors listen to radio and receive WhatsApp voice notes from family, but few use apps or read small text. Which concept do you select?
options: A detailed 20-page PDF guide with small print, posted on the Council's website.
A series of short voice-note messages and a large-print, one-page checklist that families can share, plus a radio segment.

questions.topic: The creative process applied to Caribbean problems
questions.stem: Before the full launch, what do you do?
options: Pilot the voice notes and checklist with fifteen seniors and ask them to explain back the three key steps.
Launch to the whole island immediately; there is no time to test.

questions.stem:
A Lower Six group is planning to film their school's Sports Day. Sort each planning item.

Which pre-production element is this?

Booking two cameras and four charged batteries from the media room.
questions.explain: Equipment is a resource.

questions.stem:
Which pre-production element is this?

Getting parents to sign release forms for students who will be interviewed.
questions.explain: Releases are clearances. Minors need a parent's or guardian's signature.

questions.stem:
Which pre-production element is this?

Taping down extension cables near the finish line.
questions.explain: Preventing trips is a health and safety control.

questions.stem:
Which pre-production element is this?

Licensing a royalty-free soca track for the highlights video.
questions.explain: Music must be cleared for copyright.

questions.stem:
Which pre-production element is this?

Assigning roles: director, two camera operators, sound, editor.
questions.explain: Personnel are a resource.

questions.stem:
Which pre-production element is this?

Bringing water, umbrellas and sunscreen for a midday shoot in the sun.
questions.explain: Protecting the crew from heat is health and safety.

questions.stem:
Which pre-production element is this?

Asking the principal for written permission to fly a drone over the field.
questions.explain: Permission (and possibly aviation authorisation) is a clearance.

questions.stem:
Which pre-production element is this?

Setting a three-day editing deadline after the event.
questions.explain: Time is a resource.

questions.stem:
Your school asks your group to produce a 90-second highlights video of Sports Day for the school's YouTube channel and Instagram. You have one week to plan.

What do you prepare first?
options: A brief (purpose, audience, message, platforms, deadline) and a shot list based on the event programme.
Nothing; just turn up and film whatever happens.

questions.stem: Instagram needs a vertical version and YouTube needs landscape. How do you plan capture?
options: Shoot the main camera in 16:9 at 1920 x 1080 (or 4K), framing action centrally with space to crop to 9:16, and assign one phone to shoot vertical behind-the-scenes clips.

questions.stem: You plan to interview athletes, some of them aged 13. What clearance do you arrange?
options: Ask the students to say "yes" on camera.
Send release forms home for a parent or guardian to sign, and check the school's media consent list.

questions.stem: In a student thriller set in Port of Spain, a corrupt developer threatens a shopkeeper who refuses to sell her family shop. The director wants the developer to seem powerful and menacing in his close-up. Which camera angle should she choose?
options: An eye-level shot, because it is the most realistic.
A high angle looking down on the developer.
A bird's-eye view from directly above.
A low angle looking up at the developer.

questions.stem:
A crew is filming a promotional video for a heritage festival in Grenada. Name each camera movement.

The camera stays on the tripod and turns slowly from left to right across the crowd at the market.
questions.explain: Turning horizontally on a fixed tripod is a pan.

questions.stem: The camera stays in place and pivots upward from a drummer's hands to his face.
questions.explain: Pivoting up or down from a fixed point is a tilt.

questions.stem: The camera is pushed on a slider towards the old woman as she begins her story.
questions.explain: The whole camera moves towards the subject, creating parallax: a dolly in.

questions.stem: The camera rides in a golf cart beside the dancers as they move down the street.
questions.explain: Travelling alongside a moving subject is a tracking shot.

questions.stem: The lens focal length changes so the steel pan fills the frame, but the camera does not move.
questions.explain: Only the lens changes, so there is no parallax: a zoom.

questions.stem: The camera rises on a long arm from street level to above the crowd for the final shot.
questions.explain: Rising on an arm is a crane or jib shot.

questions.stem:
A Caribbean production company is planning lighting for several projects. Sort each lighting plan by its main lighting approach.

Which lighting approach?

A bright, cheerful sitcom kitchen with soft light everywhere and almost no shadows.
questions.explain: Even, low-contrast light with strong fill is high-key: safe and comic.

questions.stem:
Which lighting approach?

A detective scene in a dark office: one hard light, deep black shadows across the walls.
questions.explain: High contrast with deep shadows is low-key: the noir look.

questions.stem:
Which lighting approach?

A night scene where a film light is hidden to look as if the glow comes from a phone screen.
questions.explain: The light imitates a believable source in the scene: motivated light.

questions.stem:
Which lighting approach?

A resort advert with bright, airy rooms and white linen, lit evenly.
questions.explain: Advertising and tourism usually choose high-key for an open, optimistic mood.

questions.stem:
Which lighting approach?

A horror short where most of the frame is black and only half the villain's face is lit.
questions.explain: Mostly dark with selective highlights is low-key.

questions.stem:
Which lighting approach?

A storytelling scene round a beach bonfire, with orange light flickering on faces from below.
questions.explain: The fire is the visible, believable source; the crew may add a flickering orange lamp to match it.

questions.stem:
Which lighting approach?

An interior where a soft light outside the window imitates morning sun streaming in.
questions.explain: Window light that the audience believes in, but which the crew controls, is motivated.

questions.stem:
The boutique tour company Sweet Isle Tours in St. Lucia hires your crew to make a 30-second promo for Instagram Reels and YouTube. The message: "Our island, your story." You must plan the shot sequence.

How do you open the promo (0 to 4 seconds)?
options: A drone extreme long shot sweeping over the Pitons at golden hour, then a quick cut to a smiling guide waving.
A medium shot of the company owner reading the price list to camera.

questions.stem: For the middle (4 to 24 seconds), what shot pattern do you plan?
options: Twenty seconds of the same wide shot of the beach.

A rhythm of varied shots: LS of a couple kayaking through mangroves, CU of laughter, ECU of cocoa tea being poured, tracking shot through Castries Market, POV from the catamaran bow. Each 2 to 3 seconds, cut on action.

questions.stem: How do you light and end the promo (24 to 30 seconds)?
options: High-key, warm daylight throughout; end on a slow dolly back from the couple at sunset, with the logo and "Book at sweetisle.example" over the final 4 seconds.
Low-key, shadowy lighting with a Dutch angle on the final shot to make it look cinematic.

questions.stem:
Sort each job according to whether a raster (pixel) or vector (path) tool suits it better.

Raster or vector?

Retouching a portrait photo for a graduation booklet.
questions.explain: Photographs are made of pixels, so retouching happens in a raster editor.

questions.stem:
Raster or vector?

A logo that must print on a pen and on a billboard.
questions.explain: Vector logos scale to any size without blurring.

questions.stem:
Raster or vector?

Removing a tourist from a beach photo with a healing brush.
questions.explain: Healing and cloning are pixel-level raster tasks.

questions.stem:
Raster or vector?

Icons for an app's menu that must look sharp on every screen.
questions.explain: Vector icons (e.g. SVG) stay crisp at every resolution.

questions.stem:
Raster or vector?

Colour-correcting 40 Carnival photos.
questions.explain: Batch photo correction is a raster task (e.g. Lightroom).

questions.stem:
Raster or vector?

A map illustration for a heritage trail brochure with clean lines and text.
questions.explain: Clean, scalable illustration with editable text suits vector tools.

questions.stem: A Barbados primary school teacher with no design training needs to make weekly illustrated newsletters and matching social media posts. She has a Chromebook, no budget and 30 minutes a week. Which tool has the GREATEST utility for her?
options: Canva (free version), because it runs in a browser, offers ready templates in several formats and is quick to learn.
GIMP, because it is free and open-source.
Adobe Illustrator, because it is the industry standard for vector graphics.
Blender, because it is free and can create 3D animation.

questions.stem:
Each statement describes an advantage or disadvantage of a tool. Identify the criterion.

"The software will not install because my laptop has only 4 GB of RAM."
questions.explain: Hardware limits such as RAM are technical requirements.

questions.stem: "The app's free plan lets the company use my uploaded photos in its advertising."
questions.explain: Terms that affect your data and ownership of your work raise privacy and copyright concerns.

questions.stem: "Files exported from this program cannot be opened by the printer's software."
questions.explain: Working with other systems and formats is compatibility.

questions.stem: "Our web tool stops working every time the school internet goes down."
questions.explain: Dependence on a connection affects reliability.

questions.stem: "Anyone with the link could view the client's unreleased footage."
questions.explain: Unprotected sharing is a security issue.

questions.stem:
Kerry-Ann is editing photos for a Jamaican coffee company's website. Name the concept she uses each time.

She hides the messy background behind a coffee bag by painting black on a layer, without erasing any pixels.
questions.explain: Hiding without deleting is a layer mask.

questions.stem: She sets a coffee-stain texture layer to Multiply so only its darker tones show over the label.
questions.explain: Multiply is a blend mode.

questions.stem: She adds a Curves layer above the photo to lift the shadows, leaving the original layer untouched.
questions.explain: A separate, editable correction is an adjustment layer.

questions.stem: She needs the company logo on a delivery van and on a business card, sharp at both sizes.
options: a vector file such as SVG
questions.explain: Vector artwork scales without losing quality.

questions.stem: She exports the product cut-out with a transparent background for the web shop.
questions.explain: PNG supports transparency and suits web graphics.

questions.stem:
Your group is producing a documentary. Choose the best sharing practice in each case.

Your client should be able to add notes on the draft script but not change it. Set the permission to...
options: anyone with the link can edit
questions.explain: Commenter lets the client add notes without altering the text.

questions.stem: An editor accidentally deleted a paragraph yesterday. The quickest fix is to...
questions.explain: Cloud tools keep version history so you can restore earlier drafts.

questions.stem: You must send 40 separate image files to a printer in one tidy package.
options: compress them into a ZIP archive
questions.explain: A ZIP archive keeps files together and reduces transfer problems.

questions.stem: Unreleased interview footage includes minors. The shared folder should be...
questions.explain: Sensitive footage should be shared only with named people.

questions.stem: Which backup plan follows the 3-2-1 rule?
options: two copies on the same memory card
questions.explain: Three copies, two kinds of storage, one off-site (the cloud).

questions.stem:
A St. Lucian tourism office is reviewing its social media posts. Sort each practice.

Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Adding accurate captions to every video.
questions.explain: Captions help Deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers and anyone watching with the sound off.

questions.stem:
Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Light yellow text on a white background.
questions.explain: Low contrast makes text hard or impossible to read. Aim for strong contrast (WCAG suggests at least 4.5:1 for body text).

questions.stem:
Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Writing alt text that describes each image.
questions.explain: Alt text lets screen-reader users understand images.

questions.stem:
Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Using colour alone (red vs green) to show which beaches are open.
questions.explain: Colour-blind users may not see the difference. Add labels or icons.

questions.stem:
Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Providing a transcript for each podcast episode.
questions.explain: Transcripts help Deaf users and make content searchable.

questions.stem:
Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Putting all important information in a decorative script font.
questions.explain: Script fonts are hard to read, especially for people with dyslexia or low vision.

questions.stem:
Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Using plain language and short sentences.
questions.explain: Plain language helps everyone, including non-native speakers.

questions.stem:
Does this practice make content more accessible or less accessible?

Rapidly flashing graphics in a promo.
questions.explain: Flashing content can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.

questions.stem:
BVI Shore Keepers needs 100 volunteers for a beach clean-up at Cane Garden Bay in three weeks. Audiences: secondary students, parents and local businesses. You run the communication plan.

How do you plan the communication?
options: Post one long text message on Facebook and hope it spreads.
Match each audience to a method: Reels and TikTok for students, a WhatsApp flyer and voice note for parents, a short professional email for businesses.

questions.stem: The volunteer flyer is ready. A teammate designed it with five fonts, red text on a green background and no date. What do you do?
options: Post it anyway; it is colourful and eye-catching.
Redesign it with two fonts, a clear hierarchy, high-contrast colours and the date, time, place and sign-up link prominent.

questions.stem: You want to live stream the clean-up on the day. What do you check first?
options: Test the mobile data upload speed at Cane Garden Bay, charge a power bank, and plan captions or on-screen text for viewers with sound off.

questions.stem: A designer in Kingston has two jobs this week: a statement letter template for a Jamaican bank, and a poster for a carnival fete. Which typeface plan is MOST appropriate?

Turquoise, teal and sea-green: three neighbours on the wheel.

Red, green and blue light at full strength make white.

The Instagram reel is edited and exported in this model.

Cyan and magenta overlap to make blue.

A fourth ink, K, is added because the other three make a muddy brown.

questions.stem: What are the three core categories of digital media?
options: Digital platforms, digitized content, and digital services
questions.explain: The notes group digital media into digital platforms, digitised content and digital services. Hardware, software and networks are the technology underneath; text, audio and images are only kinds of content.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a digital platform?
questions.explain: A website or app is a platform: the place or service through which content is delivered. An MP3 file and a digital painting are content; a compact disc is a physical storage medium.

questions.stem: Digitized content, as described in the material, includes which types of media?
questions.explain: Digitised content covers all four: text, audio, video and images. The other options leave types out, and hardware and software are not content.

questions.stem: Which software titles are named as commonly used for Computer Generated Graphics (CGI)?
options: Photoshop, Procreate, and Clip Studio Paint
questions.explain: Blender, Maya and Cinema 4D are 3D and CGI programs. Photoshop, Procreate and Clip Studio Paint are 2D painting tools, Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve edit video, and Audacity and Logic Pro edit audio.

questions.stem: Digital painting is typically created using:
options: A scanner and photo editing software
A graphics tablet and painting software
questions.explain: Digital painting is created directly on a device, usually with a graphics tablet and painting software. A scanner turns a physical painting into digitised artwork instead.

questions.stem: What is giclée printing?
options: A high-quality digital inkjet process used to reproduce original artwork
questions.explain: Giclée is a high-quality inkjet printing process, with archival inks, used to reproduce original artwork as fine-art prints.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes hybrid artwork?
options: It blends traditional fine art techniques with digital methods such as printmaking or sketching
It is art created entirely by artificial intelligence
It refers only to artwork printed on canvas
It is music combined with visual art
questions.explain: Hybrid artwork blends traditional fine-art techniques, such as printmaking or sketching, with digital methods. AI-only art and canvas prints are something else.

questions.stem: What distinguishes 3D art from 2D art?
options: 3D art is always animated while 2D art never is
2D art can only be created in black and white
3D art has height, width, and depth, while 2D art has only height and width
questions.explain: 3D art has height, width and depth; 2D art has only height and width. 3D art need not be animated, and both can be produced digitally.

questions.stem: How is digital audio defined in the material?
options: Sound stored only on vinyl records
A type of video file format
Sound represented as numerical, binary values
questions.explain: Digital audio is sound that has been sampled and stored as numbers (binary values). Vinyl stores sound as physical grooves, which is analogue.

questions.stem: Which digital audio format is uncompressed and best suited to professional audio production and editing?
questions.explain: WAV is uncompressed, so it keeps full quality for recording and editing. MP3, AAC and OGG are lossy compressed formats.

questions.stem: Which audio format is closely associated with Apple devices, iTunes, and YouTube audio?
questions.explain: AAC is the default format for Apple devices and iTunes and is also used for YouTube audio.

questions.stem: How does a compact disc (CD) store audio data?
options: As microscopic pits on its surface, read by a laser
As magnetic patterns on a tape
As binary code on a hard drive
As grooves cut by a needle
questions.explain: A CD stores audio as microscopic pits read by a laser. Tape is magnetic, and grooves cut by a needle describe vinyl records.

questions.stem: Which animation technique involves photographing physical objects one frame at a time?
questions.explain: Stop motion photographs physical objects one frame at a time, moving them slightly between shots.

questions.stem: Which type of animation uses CGI software to build three-dimensional characters and environments?
questions.explain: 3D animation builds three-dimensional characters and environments in CGI software, then animates and renders them.

questions.stem: Motion graphics, as described in the material, are commonly used for:
options: Explainer videos, UI, and broadcast media
questions.explain: Motion graphics animate text, shapes and icons, and are common in explainer videos, user interfaces (UI) and broadcast media such as news titles.

questions.stem: What are the three stages of digital video production described in the material?
questions.explain: The notes describe three stages: capture, editing and production (output). In Module 3 you will also meet the industry model of pre-production, production and post-production.

questions.stem: Which software titles are named as commonly used for video editing?
options: Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve, and Final Cut
questions.explain: Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve and Final Cut are video editors. Blender, Maya and ZBrush are 3D tools, and Audacity and GarageBand are audio tools.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a multimedia mobile app?
options: An app that blends video, audio, text, and graphics into a rich, interactive experience
questions.explain: A multimedia app blends video, audio, text and graphics into an interactive experience. A calculator, alarm or plain notes app uses a single medium for a single job.

questions.stem: What do social media apps primarily enable, according to the material?
options: Sharing, creating, and consuming digital content across communities
questions.explain: Social media apps let communities share, create and consume content. They are not limited to messaging, photo storage or streaming.

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes how the material describes digital media overall?
options: It is an interconnected ecosystem where art, audio, video, animation, and interactive technology converge
It is a single, unified file format
It refers exclusively to social media platforms
It refers only to entertainment content
questions.explain: The notes describe digital media as an interconnected ecosystem in which art, audio, video, animation and interactive technology converge. It is not one file format, and it is not only social or entertainment media.

questions.stem: Digital media only refers to social media platforms.
questions.explain: False. Digital media covers far more than social media: digital art, audio, video, animation, apps, websites and games.

questions.stem: Digitized artwork refers to traditional physical works converted into digital format through scanning or high-resolution photography.
questions.explain: True. Digitised artwork starts as a physical work and is scanned or photographed at high resolution.

questions.stem: 2D art is composed in three dimensions: height, width, and depth.
questions.explain: False. Height, width and depth describe 3D art; 2D art has only height and width.

questions.stem: MP3 is an example of a compressed (lossy) audio format.
questions.explain: True. MP3 is lossy: it removes sound data the ear is less likely to notice, to make files smaller.

questions.stem: A CD is an example of a purely non-physical digital audio file.
questions.explain: False. A CD is a physical disc that stores digital audio; it is not a non-physical file.

questions.stem: Stop motion animation involves photographing physical objects one frame at a time.
questions.explain: True. Stop motion moves and photographs physical objects one frame at a time.

questions.stem: WAV files are compressed and lossy.
questions.explain: False. WAV files are normally uncompressed, so they are large and keep full quality.

questions.stem: Motion graphics involve animated text, shapes, and icons.
questions.explain: True. Motion graphics animate text, shapes and icons.

questions.stem: Digital video editing can only be done non-destructively using magnetic tape.
questions.explain: False. Digital editing is done in software and is non-destructive; tape editing was physical and linear.

questions.stem: Mobile apps can combine audio, video, art, and interactivity in a single portable experience.
questions.explain: True. Mobile apps can combine audio, video, art and interactivity in one portable experience.
